cards.title: Additive-one approximation for bin packing
cards.formal:
Is there a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for one-dimensional offline bin packing that uses at most one more bin than optimum? Explicitly allowing randomization, the target is one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every finite input list \(I=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n})\) of rational sizes \(0<s_{i}\le1\), \(A\) runs within \(p(L)\) steps for every coin sequence, always outputs a feasible packing, and satisfies
\[
\Pr\bigl[B(A(I))\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)+1\bigr]\ge\tfrac23.
\]
Here \(L\) is the total binary input length, \(B\) is the number of bins used, and probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair random bits for each fixed input. A deterministic algorithm with the same bound on every input also qualifies.
cards.why: A one-extra-bin algorithm would show that a strongly NP-hard packing problem can nevertheless be solved to a uniformly tiny additive error. The question tests a much sharper notion of approximation than a ratio tending to one and is a long-standing benchmark for understanding the structure of feasible packings.
cards.status_note: Checked the complete two-page source question and the full Hoberg–Rothvoss author manuscript, especially Theorem 2 and its expected-time randomization convention. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no algorithm achieving the stated one-extra-bin target; newer results for online, dynamic or other packing variants do not establish it. The dated known bound is not presented as a newly proved 2026 theorem.
cards.review_note: Defined explicit binary rational inputs, offline packing output, integer optimum, exact capacity, additive-one guarantee and uniform bit complexity. Explicitly allows bounded-error randomization; preserves the source’s constant-additive discussion as partial progress.

sentences: Bin packing assigns indivisible items of known sizes to bins of unit capacity.
The goal is to find a packing that uses at most one bin more than the minimum possible.
The algorithm must run in polynomial time in the complete binary input length.
Known general algorithms achieve a logarithmic additive loss, while approximation schemes do not guarantee one extra bin.
The question asks how closely efficient computation can approach the exact optimum of a fundamental packing problem.

cards.definitions:
All items and their sizes are given before computation starts. Each item is listed separately, including repetitions. Write \(s_{i}=a_{i}/b_{i}\), where \(a_{i},b_{i}\) are positive binary integers and \(a_{i}\le b_{i}\). Input length includes the item list, numerators, denominators and separators; arithmetic precision is not free.

A packing partitions the item indices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) into nonempty bins \(B_{1},\ldots,B_{q}\) such that
\[
\sum_{i\in B_{j}}s_{i}\le1\quad\text{for every }j.
\]
Items are indivisible and must each appear in exactly one bin. The output explicitly assigns every item to a bin. The integer \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum feasible number \(q\); the empty input has optimum zero and can be packed in zero bins. Zero-size items, if allowed by an alternative convention, can be handled separately without changing the existence question.

Running time is worst-case bit complexity on a uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine. There is no input advice, supplied optimal packing or promise on the size distribution, number of distinct sizes or optimum. The input is an explicit list, not binary multiplicities representing exponentially many separate output items.

The additive allowance is exactly one bin with capacity exactly 1. It does not grow with the instance, and it is not a multiplicative factor \(1+\varepsilon\). Neither larger bin capacities nor discarding an item is permitted. The target concerns the integer optimum of the packing problem, not the optimum of a fractional relaxation.

The probability convention makes explicit an algorithmic interpretation that includes randomized approximation algorithms, as in the later logarithmic-additive result. Its theorem gives expected polynomial runtime with its quality guarantee; that is a separately reported form of the known result. For the target here, the output must always be feasible and only the one-extra-bin guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give one algorithm and a proof of all stated time, feasibility and probability guarantees, or refute the existence of such an algorithm. A conditional impossibility result must expose its assumption, including any assumption needed to exclude randomized algorithms. An \(\operatorname{OPT}+C\) bound with unspecified constant \(C>1\), an asymptotic approximation scheme, or a nonconstructive fractional-integrality-gap bound alone does not meet the target.

context_blocks.title: One extra bin is the source’s endpoint
context_blocks.text: Problem 3 asks whether bin packing can join problems that admit polynomial-time solutions within one unit of their integer optimum. The book separately highlights a constant number of extra bins as significant progress. This card keeps the one-bin endpoint as its main target.

context_blocks.title: The historical logarithmic-squared bound improved
context_blocks.text: The book recalls the Karmarkar–Karp additive \(O((\log n)^{2})\) guarantee. Hoberg and Rothvoss later give a randomized algorithm with expected polynomial runtime and at most \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+O(\log(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+2))\) bins, where \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\le\operatorname{OPT}\) is the fractional packing optimum. In particular this gives \(\operatorname{OPT}+O(\log(\operatorname{OPT}+2))\) bins, without establishing a constant additive bound.

context_blocks.title: Fractional packing is a related comparison
context_blocks.text: The Gilmore–Gomory relaxation permits a nonnegative fractional number of copies of each feasible bin pattern and requires enough total coverage of each item type. Its objective is the total fractional number of bins. Statements comparing its optimum to integer packings concern an integrality gap; an existence bound for that gap does not by itself specify the efficient algorithm required here.

context_blocks.title: Asymptotic ratios do not fix the additive allowance
context_blocks.text: Bounds of the form \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}+C_{\varepsilon}\) can approach multiplicative ratio 1 while retaining an unbounded or larger additive loss. They therefore do not imply the requested one-extra-bin guarantee on every instance.

cards.context:
Problem 3 asks whether bin packing can join problems that admit polynomial-time solutions within one unit of their integer optimum. The book separately highlights a constant number of extra bins as significant progress. This card keeps the one-bin endpoint as its main target.

The book recalls the Karmarkar–Karp additive \(O((\log n)^{2})\) guarantee. Hoberg and Rothvoss later give a randomized algorithm with expected polynomial runtime and at most \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+O(\log(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+2))\) bins, where \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\le\operatorname{OPT}\) is the fractional packing optimum. In particular this gives \(\operatorname{OPT}+O(\log(\operatorname{OPT}+2))\) bins, without establishing a constant additive bound.

The Gilmore–Gomory relaxation permits a nonnegative fractional number of copies of each feasible bin pattern and requires enough total coverage of each item type. Its objective is the total fractional number of bins. Statements comparing its optimum to integer packings concern an integrality gap; an existence bound for that gap does not by itself specify the efficient algorithm required here.

Bounds of the form \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}+C_{\varepsilon}\) can approach multiplicative ratio 1 while retaining an unbounded or larger additive loss. They therefore do not imply the requested one-extra-bin guarantee on every instance.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
